races.note: Incumbent Josh Green (D) vs. Gary Cordery (R). No U.S. Senate race in 2026. Rated Solid/Safe D by Cook, Inside Elections and Sabato.
Ranked-choice voting for Honolulu mayor, city council and prosecuting attorney in a single November election, from 2032, if the Legislature also approves. Yes = adopt RCV.

assessment.threshold: Majority of voters voting on the question. Blank votes don’t count, unlike Hawaii constitutional amendments
assessment.summary: The data puts this close to a coin flip, leaning Yes. Across 10 local RCV votes, an electorate as Democratic as Oʻahu’s (Harris 61%) would be expected to give about 54% Yes. Honolulu’s four past charter amendments on how officials are elected averaged 52.7%, though they ranged from 35% to 83%. Averaging the two gives about 53%, roughly a 64% chance of passing. The local track record is the thinnest of the three cities’, so treat this one with the most caution.
for: Supported by the Democratic Party of Hawaiʻi and the League of Women Voters of Hawaiʻi
The Star-Advertiser editorial board recommends Yes
Blank votes are excluded, so the many voters who skip down-ballot charter questions don’t count as No
Delayed to 2032 and contingent on the Legislature, which softens the ‘too fast, too costly’ argument
Hawaii already uses ranked ballots in some special federal and county elections
against: The Hawaii Republican Party (Chair Shirlene Ostrov, Rep. Elijah Pierick) is actively opposing it, and a Star-Advertiser op-ed called RCV something that ‘ruins elections’
It eliminates the familiar primary-plus-general format for city offices
Voters face 20 charter questions, and ballot fatigue pushes undecided voters toward No
RCV measures in large electorates have underperformed partisanship (Oregon 2024: 42%, Colorado 2024: 46.5%)
assessment.finance: Hawaii Campaign Spending Commission data through Sept. 30 shows no ballot-issue committee for or against Question 5. FairVote Action, the national pro-RCV group, reported two Hawaii payments: $2,900 to the Democratic Party of Hawaii for its voter file (Sept. 11) and $31,750 to the pollster FM3 (Sept. 23). The filing describes the FM3 payment only as “Poll.” It doesn’t say the poll was about Question 5, though that’s the only RCV question on a Hawaii ballot this year. Sept. 23 is the payment date, not necessarily when the poll was in the field. The results haven’t been released, and groups often keep internal polls private regardless of what they find. The Hawaii GOP’s reported spending (mostly digital ads and email) isn’t itemized by issue.

model.anchor_label: Honolulu’s past charter amendments on electing officials
model.anchor_detail: Four Honolulu charter amendments since 2010 changed how city officials are elected: term limits for city offices (36.7%), nonpartisan reapportionment commission (35.4%), special election time extension (55.5%), term limits for prosecuting attorney (83.2%), averaging 52.7%. All 42 Honolulu charter amendments since 2010 averaged 64.0% and 83% passed.

assessment.turnout: Hawaii doesn’t publish daily returns in a form this site can read for Oʻahu alone, so no turnout adjustment was made.
